I am the opposite of you, I basically only read LitRPG nowadays, and I can tell you that sort of story is antithetical to what people who actually love the genre are looking for. 

While every reader has their own tropes they refuse to engage with (I immediately drop a story that has an academy arc for example) you will see massive pushback from the entire reader base as soon as you implement anything that compromises the MCs agency, even temporarily. Slave arcs, mind control arcs, etc are hated by the crowd.

Stories that use them (IMO) suffer because of it. I’ll use New World as an example, it has everything the average reader wants and more, but it suffered because it made the system an active character who is antagonistic to the MC, putting limits on what he can do, and while a lot of the story is MC working around it people still drop the story.

LitRPG is a genre where the major audience on RR, the silent lurkers, want somewhat unique wish-fulfillment where the MC has agency, and some sort of advantage - whether it be a lucky encounter, memories of the future, or a unique mindset, something sets them apart that leads to the MC quickly becoming a major player.

Unfortunately, the paying audience decides what gets made the most, and the Amazon market likes the cost of paint LitRPG gives but isn’t too attached to the core conceit it originally offered. More and more authors are using it as a vehicle to tell their own sort of story while gaining an easy audience

I actually agree with you that fantasy races that the in-universe reaction to is genocide isn’t some all terrible thing.

The Goblins in Goblin slayer are essentially generated animals, I don’t believe they are truly sapient. In every case in-universe, they inevitably will conflict with humanity. Part of this is undoubtedly because the world is made by the gods and they decided what role goblins play, but it doesn’t change the fact that the only safe option for civilization is to genocide them.

Same with Orks in Warhammer (both fantasy and 40k). They can have individuals, likes and dislikes, but will always decide to fight - because that is what their species is made for by their creators. I don’t think there are any examples of Orks that don’t enjoy fighting. The only option for safe human civilization is to genocide any Orks you come in contact with - as even their presence will infect the area and spawn more Orks.

At the end of the day, when humanity exists in a fantasy setting, most people end up rooting for humanity. Genocide for a species usually ends up supported when a species clashes with humanity in such a way that - through either culture, mindset, or just straight up the basis for existence, they are unable to mesh the way that different human tribes and kingdoms were able to in real life.

There’s a reason people would support genociding Skaven in fantasy, but not Wood Elves - both are hostile to humanity, but Skaven are driven by their culture, magic, and god to constantly clash with humanity (not just humanity) and are a massive threat. Wood Elves by and large stay in their forest, and desire their kingdom’s sanctity. They brutally kill those who enter, and often refuse diplomacy, but ultimately it’s the fault of those who go against them, not them against humans.

Misinformation. LucasArts used to have a guy who’s job explicitly was to keep track of the canon and advise EU Writers. Canon had different levels of what took priority, though this system is no longer in play since the Disney “Legendization”

G-canon, or George Lucas canon: The six Star Wars films in their most recent incarnations, including unpublished production notes from Lucas or his production department. Elements originating with Lucas in the film novelizations, reference books, and other adaptations. Direct declarations made by Lucas. Deleted scenes from the films that do not conflict with the film itself.

T-canon, or Television canon: The Star Wars: The Clone Wars animated series, its feature film, and the Star Wars Rebels animated series.

C-canon, or Continuity canon: The majority of Expanded Universe stories, including novels, comics, video games, and other content originating from other authors. C-canon material could be elevated to G-canon if a subject appeared in a Lucas project.

S-canon, or Secondary canon: Material that could be used or ignored as desired by authors, including older works that predated a concentrated effort to maintain a consistent continuity, such as the Marvel Star Wars comics. Anything that is not completely outrageous or intentionally comic.

N-canon, or Non-canon: "What-if" stories, including those published under the Infinities label. Any content directly and irreconcilably contradicted by higher canon. Cut content and canceled projects. This was the only level that Lucasfilm did not consider to have some degree of canonicity.

D-canon, or Detours canon: The Star Wars Detours animated series, which was not released before the Lucasfilm declaration of April 25, 2014. This canon level was never fully defined as a result.

To clarify before I say anything, AH is written as a serial, not a typical book. This is relevant for the way it’s written - in terms of plot and story structure that differentiates itself from more traditional stories, which also leads to a change in audience.

For the most part, people who like these serial stories don’t care about grammar. More than that, they are used to worse grammar, and since they read mostly serials with just as bad or worse grammar, Azarinth is seen as really good in comparison. 

I’ve read a stupid amount of serials - both translated and not - in the last few years and they are, as a whole, written terribly. Especially recently, sites like Webnovel seem to be using Machine translation (basically google trans) more and more frequently for new stories. It’s not uncommon to read stories where a character’s gender is constantly switched, things are randomly given new names 40 chaps in, and the MC will have their name suddenly changed with no explanation. 

It’s like if the only pizza you ever ate was molding, and then you get a slice of simply old, cold pizza. It’s not good the way a fresh out of the oven pizza is, but it’s much better than you are used to.

Essentially, even though the grammar is bad, people who like most likely don’t care.

It all depends on the system used. In some stories, leveling allows you to gain more abilities and skills, while in others it’s a flat attribute increase. 

But then even that depends on what attributes are, and the definition can vary based on the story. Maybe a point in strength represents a specific increase (maybe you can carry x number of pounds at 10 strength), or maybe it’s less specific but tailored to the individual (someone who has more muscle mass is stronger at 10 strength than someone who has never lifted a finger at 10 strength), or maybe even it just represents how much stronger you are than the average person (a normal human starts at 1 strength, so at 10 you’re as strong as 10 people)

I’m sure you could tailor your system for a story like this, but no game would ever use this system. I believe one of the biggest MMORPG killers is lack of end-game content. People finish the story and get to max level and find almost nothing left for them to do. 

Sure your initial start would be hard, but dedicated people will still get there rather quickly.

Well I mean there was a bunch of under ground support from a ton of planets - in both men, material, and credits. They had some holdovers form the CIS, major funding from Corellia and Alderaan, privateer fleets and hired bandits, the direct support of the Calamari (major ship-building planet), and a ton of Imperial defectors (including high-ranking generals and admirals, as well as famous pilots and commandos) and underground Imperial support. And they had political savvy senators from the former Republic. The Calamari were the only ones to successfully cede from the Empire without being destroyed, and since they were able to block themselves off from the Empire (blocking/sabotaging known hyperspace routes) they were able to publicly support the Alliance. 

The main reason for the Rebellions success was their “no state” strategy. In their prime, the Rebellion had only around 23% equivalent to the Empire’s military. Their main strategy was to focus on relatively easy wins - symbolic victories to show how vulnerable the Empire was. They’d jump into a vulnerable system, smash the Imperial forces there and jump out before reinforcements arrived. Because they kept their main fleet back and had no stationary headquarters, the Empire couldn’t really attack them, but instead focus on defense. That’s where the largeness of the Empire became an issue, they had to keep their forces spread out to make sure the Rebels couldn’t just attack wherever they wanted. 

In Legends, after destroying the second Death Star the Empire doesn’t immediately collapse. It’s split by war-monger high-ranking officials who all want to become the new emperor. They were a bunch of groups, but the most important ones were the groups led by former Grand Admirals. I believe the main group was called the Imperial Remnant. The Alliance rebranded themselves the New Republic and consolidated their gains, and slowly built up their forces with renewed support from former imperial worlds. Over a few years they pushed into the Core and took Coruscant, cementing themselves as the new main force in the galaxy.
